stories.title: Do Static Types Really Prevent Bugs?
alternates: Static vs Dynamic Typing: What the Experiments Show
The Language-Bug Study That Fell Apart
stories.question: Do static types actually save you time and bugs?
stories.whyWatch: The typing argument is usually settled by taste. Controlled experiments, a check of real JavaScript bugs, and a failed replication of the most cited repository study show what types do and do not buy.
stories.tension: Fans say types catch bugs before users do; skeptics say most bugs are not type errors and dynamic languages are faster to write. Both have some evidence.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Controlled experiments on type-error fixing, a measure of how many real bugs a type checker would catch, the replication of the repository-scale study, and development-time comparisons.
evidenceAvailable: Berger et al. 2019 (languages reproduction): right (0.75, direct)
Kleinschmager et al. 2012 (static types): right (0.6, direct)
Hanenberg et al. 2014 (static types): right (0.6, direct)
Gao, Bird & Barr 2017 (types vs JS bugs): right (0.5, direct)
Kleinschmager et al. 2012 (static types): right (0.65, partial)
Hanenberg et al. 2014 (static types): right (0.65, partial)
Prechelt 2000 (seven languages): partly (0.45, partial)
Hanenberg et al. 2014 (static types): partly (0.3, direct)
Ray et al. 2014 (languages on GitHub): partly (0.2, partial)
gaps: Ray et al. 2014 (languages on GitHub) is context only: observational bug-fix counts from a corpus whose TypeScript sample Berger et al. later showed was mislabelled; it cannot decide what a compiler catches
stories.premise: In Kleinschmager et al.'s controlled experiment the Java version of a type-error task failed to compile while the Groovy version only failed at run time, and the static side won on time: 78 against 149 seconds and 44 against 246 seconds on the two type-error tasks. Hanenberg et al.'s journal version found every indicator favoured static types on those tasks because the compiler names the location while a run-time failure can appear far from the cause. Those experiments used a compiler, not an in-editor checker; an editor shows the same message sooner, but that was not what was tested. Gao, Bird and Barr annotated 400 fixed public JavaScript bugs and the type checker flagged 15% of them, so most bugs are not type errors. Ray et al.'s 729-project GitHub study, which linked languages to defect rates, did not survive Berger et al.'s reanalysis: mislabelled files, duplicated projects, 36% false-positive bug labels and no multiple-testing correction left 4 of 11 associations with very small effects. On prototyping, Prechelt's scripts took a median 3.1 hours against 10.0 for C, C++ and Java, but on one problem, with self-reported script times, and the author credits built-in associative arrays rather than typing; Hanenberg's own series has tasks going each way.

arc.hook: Every few months the static-versus-dynamic argument flares up again, usually citing a big study that says language choice changes your bug rate.
arc.conflict: Types clearly catch some errors earlier, but how many bugs are type errors, and does the extra ceremony slow you down?
arc.evidence: The type-error experiments and their timings, the 15% of real JavaScript bugs a checker would have flagged, the failed replication of the GitHub study, and the prototyping comparison with its caveats.
arc.resolution: Static types find type errors sooner and point at them, which makes those fixes faster; they catch a minority of real bugs; the repository-scale claims about whole languages did not hold up; and the speed advantage for dynamic languages is narrow and confounded.
arc.takeaway: Choose static types for the faster, located feedback on type errors, not for a promise of fewer bugs overall.

coherence.explanation: One question, do static types pay off: errors caught before running, how much faster the fix is, the repository-scale bug claims that fell apart, and the prototyping speed argued for dynamic typing. The runtime performance claim is a separate question with only a qualified, implementation-bound verdict, so it is pruned; the in-editor feedback claim is folded in from its own candidate.

stories.title: Are Small Pull Requests Really Better?
alternates: How Big Should a Pull Request Be?
What Google's Review Data Say About Change Size
stories.question: Do small pull requests really get reviewed faster and break less?
stories.whyWatch: Keep your PRs small is the most repeated code-review advice. Review data from GitHub, Google, Microsoft and an industrial team show which part of it holds and which numbers nobody has measured.
stories.tension: Small changes are said to be reviewed faster, reviewed better and to break less. The data back the first, show reviewers giving less per line on big changes without the sharp cliff the advice describes, and tie size to failures only as risk per change.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Review-to-merge time by change size, defect-finding by review size, and incident rates by change size.

dos Santos & Nunes 2018 (review and patch size): right (0.5, partial)
Sadowski et al. 2018 (Google code review): right (0.55, partial)
dos Santos & Nunes 2018 (review and patch size): partly (0.3, partial)
Bosu et al. 2015 (useful review comments): partly (0.3, partial)
McIntosh et al. 2014 (review coverage): partly (0.35, direct)
Sadowski et al. 2018 (Google code review): partly (0.3, direct)
Mockus & Weiss 2000 (change risk): partly (0.4, partial)
DORA State of DevOps 2019: partly (0.4, partial)
gaps: No study strong enough to decide: "Reviewer defect-finding effectiveness drops sharply once a single review exceeds a few hundred lines"
No study strong enough to decide: "Smaller changes mean less rework, fewer incidents and faster restoration"
stories.premise: Across about 40,000 merged pull requests in 40 GitHub projects, those adding more lines and commits took significantly longer from creation to close; at Google small changes get first reviewer feedback in under an hour against about five hours for very large ones; and in one 201-person industrial project larger patches took longer to reach final approval, though size explained little of the variance. These are associations in observational data, not experiments. On review quality, comments per 100 lines fall as patches grow (levelling off past about 600 lines) and the share of comments Microsoft authors found useful falls gradually with the number of files; neither counts defects found, and nothing here shows effectiveness dropping sharply past a few hundred lines, while at Google comments per change keep rising up to about 1,250 lines. On breakage, in a telecom system a change with more added lines and more subsystems touched was more likely to cause a failure, and DORA links extra approvals to larger batches and higher change failure; that is risk per change, not proof that splitting work lowers total failures, and rework and restoration time by change size are unmeasured.

arc.hook: Every code-review guide says keep your pull requests small. Is that advice measured, or just repeated?
arc.conflict: The advice bundles three promises: small changes get reviewed faster, get reviewed better past a line-count cliff, and break less. Each rests on different evidence.
arc.evidence: GitHub pull-request latency and Google first-feedback times for speed; comment density and comment usefulness by change size for review quality; a telecom change-risk model and DORA for failures.
arc.resolution: Speed holds: bigger changes take longer to get through review in every dataset here, as an association. Reviewers do give less per line on bigger changes, but gradually, and the few-hundred-lines cliff is not measured. Bigger changes carry more failure risk each; whether splitting them cuts total failures, rework or restore time is not shown.
arc.takeaway: Keep changes small to get them reviewed and merged sooner and to give reviewers less to skim; treat any exact line limit as a rule of thumb, not a finding.

coherence.explanation: The group mixed pairing and mobbing beliefs with change size; pruned to one question, should you keep changes small for review. The pairing and mob claims are unchecked beliefs and the pair-review claim rests on a 0.25 recommendation.

stories.title: Does Test-Driven Development Actually Make Better Code?
alternates: Test First or Test After: Does the Order Matter?
What Happened When Researchers Put TDD to the Test
stories.question: Does writing tests first actually give you better code than writing them right after?
stories.whyWatch: TDD is sold as the discipline that makes code better, and plenty of teams require it. Controlled experiments with students and professionals checked whether the test-first order is what makes the difference.
stories.tension: Advocates say test-first forces better design and fewer bugs. The experiments compared it with writing tests in small steps straight after the code and could not tell the two apart.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Controlled comparisons of TDD against a disciplined test-last practice on quality and productivity, plus a review of the wider literature.
evidenceAvailable: Fucci et al. 2016 (TDD replication): right (0.6, direct)
Fucci et al. 2017 (TDD dissection): right (0.55, direct)
Karac & Turhan 2018 (TDD review): right (0.5, direct)
stories.premise: Fucci et al. 2016 ran a blind-analysis crossover replication with 21 graduate students and found no difference between TDD and incremental test-last in tests written, external quality or productivity, with negligible effect sizes. Fucci et al. 2017 analysed 82 task sessions by 39 professionals and found that the test-first order dropped out of both the quality and the productivity models; the authors conclude test-first and test-last could be equally effective when done in equally small, steady cycles. Karac and Turhan's 2018 review of 15 years of studies finds no convincing evidence that TDD consistently beats other iterative methods. The limits: the comparison is with a disciplined test-last practice, not with writing no tests; the tasks were short; and long-term maintenance was not measured.

arc.hook: Many teams treat writing the test first as the rule that separates good engineers from the rest.
arc.conflict: If test-first is what makes code better, an experiment that changes only the order should show it.
arc.evidence: The 2016 replication with graduate students, the 2017 study of professionals where order dropped out of the models, and the 2018 review of 15 years of results.
arc.resolution: Against testing in small steps right after the code, test-first made no measurable difference to quality or productivity; the short cycle, not the order, is what the studies point to.
arc.takeaway: Write tests in small, steady steps; whether each test comes first or second is a matter of taste, not quality.

coherence.explanation: One question: does writing the test first produce better code or faster work than testing in small steps afterwards? Three independent studies answer it.

stories.title: Are 10x Programmers Real?
alternates: Where the 10x Programmer Number Really Comes From
How Much Faster Is the Fastest Programmer, Really?
stories.question: Are 10x programmers real, or is that number a myth?
stories.whyWatch: The 10x programmer shapes hiring, pay and how people judge themselves. A reanalysis of 61 experiments traces the famous figure to its source and measures the typical gap.
stories.tension: Everyone has met a programmer who seems ten times faster, and the 28:1 figure is quoted as proof. The data behind it are thin, and the typical gap is far smaller.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Work-time distributions from many controlled programming experiments, the original source of the 28:1 figure, and other examples of repeated figures that did not hold up.
evidenceAvailable: Prechelt 1999 (28:1 legend): partly (0.55, direct)
Prechelt 2000 (seven languages): partly (0.35, direct)
Prechelt 1999 (28:1 legend): partly (0.5, direct)
Dybå & Dingsøyr 2008 (agile review): partly (0.4, direct)
Berger et al. 2019 (languages reproduction): partly (0.35, direct)
stories.premise: Prechelt's 1999 reanalysis of 61 experiments with 614 subjects finds that the slowest quarter of programmers typically takes 2 to 3 times as long as the fastest quarter, rarely more than 4, and that best-against-worst ratios above 10 are rare. So differences between people are real and larger than most experimental effects, but ten times is the extreme pairing, not the typical gap. stories.question: Does high test coverage mean your tests will catch your bugs?
stories.whyWatch: Coverage is the number teams put on dashboards and gate merges on. A large experiment checked whether a higher number means a suite actually catches more faults.
stories.tension: Coverage feels like a measure of safety, but it only counts lines that ran, not whether any test would notice them being wrong.
stories.evidenceNeeded: A controlled measure of coverage against fault detection with suite size held fixed, and evidence on what a trusted suite does for delivery.

Unchecked: "Writing a test per method and mocking every dependency couples tests to implementation so refactoring breaks them"
stories.premise: Inozemtseva and Holmes generated 31,000 test suites for five large Java systems and measured how many mutants (artificially injected faults) each suite caught. stories.question: Does the way a team is organised predict bugs better than the code itself?
stories.whyWatch: Teams hunt bugs with complexity metrics, coverage and churn. Microsoft's own data found that measures of who worked on the code predicted failures better than any of them.
stories.tension: You would expect the code to be the best guide to where its bugs are. In Windows, the organisation behind the code was a better one.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Head-to-head prediction of defect-prone components from organisational and code metrics, and replications outside one company.

Bird et al. 2011 (code ownership): right (0.5, partial)
McIntosh et al. 2014 (review coverage): right (0.4, partial)
stories.premise: Nagappan et al. built defect predictors for 3,404 Windows Vista binaries. Eight organisational metrics, such as how many engineers and teams touched a binary, predicted failure-prone binaries with 86.2% precision and 84.0% recall, against 78.6 and 79.9 for churn, 79.3 and 66.0 for complexity, 74.4 and 69.9 for dependencies, 83.8 and 54.4 for coverage, and 73.8 and 62.9 for pre-release bugs. That is one system at one company. Bird et al. found that in Vista and Windows 7 the number of minor contributors to a binary correlated with failures more strongly than any other metric Microsoft collects. McIntosh et al. found the same ownership measures added explanatory power to every defect model in three open-source systems, Qt, VTK and ITK, while size mattered in two and complexity in none. These are predictions and correlations; they show where bugs concentrate, not that reorganising removes them.

arc.hook: If you had to guess which part of a huge codebase would break next, you would look at the code.

stories.tension: The open office is sold as a trade: less quiet, more collaboration. The measurements suggest you can lose the collaboration as well.

stories.title: Are Story Points More Accurate Than Hours?
alternates: Story Points vs Hours: Which Lands Closer?
Does Estimating in Points Make You More Accurate?
stories.question: Are story points actually more accurate than estimating in hours?
stories.whyWatch: Teams switch to story points because hours estimates keep failing. The research on relative estimation says whether points fix the accuracy problem.
stories.tension: Points are pitched as the honest way to estimate uncertain work. The studies find no general accuracy gain, and a specific bias when tasks differ a lot in size.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Comparisons of relative and absolute time predictions on accuracy, and evidence on when relative estimates go wrong.
evidenceAvailable: Halkjelsvik & Jørgensen 2018 (Time Predictions): wrong (0.5, direct)
stories.premise: Halkjelsvik and Jørgensen's 2018 review of time-prediction research finds few studies comparing relative and absolute methods: relative predictions improved accuracy in some contexts and worsened it in others, and in general they do not seem more accurate. When tasks differ a lot in size, people judge them more similar than they are, so a task ten times larger than the reference tends to be underestimated more with relative methods. Relative methods may still simplify estimating and reduce the need to know who will do the work. The evidence base is thin and the review does not single out complex or uncertain work, so the honest statement is that the evidence does not show points to be more accurate, not that they are worse.

arc.hook: Your team stopped estimating in hours because the hours were always wrong. Are the points any better?
arc.conflict: Relative sizing is supposed to suit uncertain work; does it actually land closer to reality?
arc.evidence: The review's summary of the relative-versus-absolute studies, and the size-assimilation bias it describes.
arc.resolution: Relative estimates are not generally more accurate than hours, and they skew when a task is much bigger or smaller than the reference.
arc.takeaway: Use points for convenience if you like, but do not expect them to fix accuracy, and compare tasks of similar size.
